notes: **Presenter:** Joshua. One person, one list, in video order.

**Before recording anything:** the Qube team connects Claude to Qube on Joshua's laptop (Claude in the Terminal app) and gives him a Qube login in Chrome. Don't show any install commands, API keys, emails, account names or numbers.

**Recording order for the screen clips** (one run, they build on each other): A1 download → A4 → A5 → A6 → A7 → A9 → A10 → A10b → A11. Record A4 to A11 as one long screen recording if you can, then take the screenshots named in each row.

**The paper:** Mebane T. Faber, "A Quantitative Approach to Tactical Asset Allocation" (2007), free on SSRN. Its rule: buy when the monthly closing price is above its 10-month simple moving average, sell and hold cash when it's below, checked once a month at the last close. Only this rule is used. No number from the paper is said or shown.

**What it's tested on:** SPY (the S&P 500 fund) if Qube has it. If not, the 10 biggest US stocks: AAPL, MSFT, NVDA, AMZN, GOOGL, META, TSLA, AVGO, JPM, BRK.B (J020's set). Neither is said out loud; the backtest screen shows it.

open.text: **Paper pick.** Faber (2007) is the Director's pick: free on SSRN, one rule Qube can build. Swap it if you'd rather show a different paper; the script doesn't name it, so only A1, A5–A7 and the CHECK steps change.
**Recording setup.** Is Qube connected to Claude on Joshua's laptop, and does Qube have SPY? If not SPY, A9 uses the 10 biggest US stocks.
**SSRN download.** If SSRN makes Joshua sign in to download the PDF, he stops at A1 step 2 and asks you.

rows.how: 1. Phone vertical (9:16), eye level, plain office wall behind him, office lights on, lock focus and exposure. 2. Frame him in the bottom two-thirds, with empty wall above his head (the inserts go there). 3. Hold a handheld mic if one is in the office, as the original does; if not, no mic. 4. Record the hook twice, clean. 5. Record lines 1–10 in one take, calm, no rush between lines. 6. Record "That's when everything changes." three more times, a little slower, looking straight into the lens.

1. Chrome, open https://ssrn.com/abstract=962461. 2. Click "Download This Paper" (or "Open PDF in Browser"). If SSRN asks you to sign in, use "Download as guest" if it's offered; if not, tell Mark and stop. 3. Save the PDF as `faber-2007.pdf`. 4. Make a new folder on the Desktop named `paper` and move `faber-2007.pdf` into it. 5. Open the PDF in Preview, page 1, zoom so the page fills the screen. 6. Screenshot page 1 (Cmd+Shift+4, then Space, click the Preview window). **CHECK: the title "A Quantitative Approach to Tactical Asset Allocation" and "Mebane T. Faber" must both be readable. If the journal name (The Journal of Wealth Management) is on the page, keep it in.** **CHECK: if any return, Sharpe, drawdown or volatility number from the paper is readable in the screenshot (in the abstract or anywhere else), the editor crops it out or blurs it. Nothing from the paper's results goes on screen.**

1. Pexels, search exactly: `reading pile of books`. 2. Pick a photo of one person reading at a desk with piles of books around them. No logos, nobody looking at the camera. 3. Not the original's photo (a woman with glasses among stacks of books in a library). 4. Crop to 1080×640.
rows.what: Old way 1: someone buried in books

rows.how: 1. Pexels, search exactly: `trader multiple monitors`. 2. Pick a photo of one person at a desk with three or more screens showing charts. No logos or brand names readable, nobody looking at the camera. 3. Not the original's photo (a man in a white shirt at a curved monitor wall). Not the J022 or J024 desk clip either. 4. Crop to 1080×640.

1. Terminal app, dark theme, font size 22, full screen. 2. Before recording, type `cd ~/Desktop/paper`, press Enter, then type `clear`, press Enter. 3. Open a Finder window on the `paper` folder and place it beside the Terminal so `faber-2007.pdf` is visible. 4. Start the screen recording (QuickTime → File → New Screen Recording, whole screen). 5. Type `claude`, press Enter. Hold 2s on the screen that shows Qube is connected. 6. Drag `faber-2007.pdf` from Finder into the Terminal window and let go. Hold 1s. **CHECK: if Claude doesn't show that Qube is connected, stop and tell Mark before going on.** **CHECK: if the file path shows his username or anything personal, tell the editor to blur it.**
rows.what: Claude starts with Qube connected, the PDF goes in

rows.how: 1. In the same Claude session, right after the PDF from A4, type exactly, by hand, don't paste. Press Shift+Enter for each new line: `Read this research paper and:` / `1. Extract the trading logic` / `2. Identify when to buy, when to sell, how much, and when to get out` / `3. Build the strategy in Qube` / `4. Backtest it on up to five years of real price data` / `5. Show me the results` / `6. Show me every single trade` / `7. Explain where the strategy might fail` / `8. Then optimize it in Qube based on those weaknesses and backtest it again` 2. Before pressing Enter, screenshot the Terminal with the whole prompt on screen (prompt.png). 3. Press Enter. **CHECK: all 8 steps must be readable in prompt.png, word for word as above. If they don't fit, make the font smaller and type it again.**

1. Keep recording while Claude reads the paper. 2. When Claude writes out the paper's rule (the 10-month moving average, the monthly check, cash when below), screenshot it (rule.png). **CHECK: the rule must be Claude's own words from this run. Don't retype or edit it. If Claude's reply quotes any return or drawdown number from the paper, tell the editor to blur that line.**

rows.file: J031_A7_qube.mp4 · 1920×1080 · up to 30s · plus J031_A7_sections.png, J031_A7_code.png
rows.how: 1. Keep recording until Claude says the strategy is built in Qube. 2. In Chrome (logged in to Qube, zoom 125%, no tabs or bookmarks showing), open the strategy Claude just built. 3. Show its sections (when to buy, when to sell, how much, when to get out). Hold 3s. Screenshot (sections.png). 4. Open its code. Hold 3s. Screenshot (code.png). **CHECK: the strategy must use the 10-month moving average and a once-a-month check, as in the paper. If Qube built something else, send Mark the screenshot before going on.**
rows.what: The strategy built in Qube, with its code

rows.how: 1. Get each logo from the project's own website or press page: Python, pandas, NumPy, matplotlib, plotly, Backtrader. 2. Canva, 3 white #FFFFFF cards, each 520×320, 16px rounded corners, logos at least 120px tall. Card 1: Python, pandas, NumPy. Card 2: matplotlib, plotly. Card 3: Backtrader. 3. Export each card as PNG. 4. In the edit, each card lands on its spoken words ("data", "charting tools", "backtesting frameworks"), stacked and offset about 60px from the one before, as the original builds its pile.

rows.file: J031_A9_backtest.mp4 · 1920×1080 · up to 20s · plus J031_A9_result.png and the dates and trade count in a note
rows.how: 1. Keep recording while Qube runs the backtest Claude set up. 2. When the result appears, hold 3s. Screenshot (result.png). 3. Open the list of every trade. Scroll top to bottom in about 3s. Hold 2s. If every trade fits on one screen, hold 3s instead of scrolling. 4. Write down for the editor, exactly as Qube shows them: the start date, the end date, and the number of trades. **CHECK: the dates must cover five years or less (Qube tests on up to five years of real price data). If the run is longer, tell Mark before the edit.** **CHECK: what's tested must be SPY, or the 10 biggest US stocks listed at the top if Qube doesn't have SPY. If it's anything else, tell Mark.** **CHECK: don't change any number Qube shows, and none of them is said out loud.**
rows.what: Qube backtest result and every trade

rows.how: 1. Back in the Terminal, keep recording until Claude answers step 7 of the prompt. 2. Scroll so the heading and at least 3 of its points are on screen together. Hold 3s. Screenshot (weaknesses.png). **CHECK: the heading and the points must be Claude's own words from this run. Don't retype or edit them.** **CHECK: if Claude names the paper's own results with numbers, tell the editor to blur those numbers.**
rows.what: Claude's "where the strategy might fail" answer

rows.file: J031_A10b_optimized.png · 1920×1080 · plus the dates and trade count in a note
rows.how: 1. Keep recording until Qube finishes at least one optimization round (step 8 of the prompt) and backtests the new version. 2. In Chrome (Qube, zoom 125%), open the strategy's version or run history so the improved version shows next to the first one. Hold 3s. Screenshot (optimized.png). 3. Write down for the editor, exactly as Qube shows them for the improved version: the start date, the end date, and the number of trades. **CHECK: it must be Qube's real result from this run. Don't change any number, and none of them is said out loud.** **CHECK: if Qube doesn't run an optimization round, stop and tell Mark before the edit, because line 7 says "then optimized".**

1. At the end of the run, scroll so Claude's time for the whole run is on screen (Claude Code shows how long it worked). If it doesn't, screenshot the clock at the start of A4 and at the end of A10b instead. 2. Screenshot (time.png). **CHECK: the time must be real, from this run, and cover the whole run including the optimization round (A10b). Don't change it. If the whole run took more than 15 minutes, tell Mark before the edit, because line 8 says "in minutes".**

Full screen 1080×1920, #0B0F14, "Comment QUBE" centred, Instrument Serif 88px white, "QUBE" in gold #E8B04B. Under it, "free sign-up link", Inter Bold 40px, light grey #9AA3AE. No quote marks, no all caps on "Comment". 2s.

lines.text: Let's code a trading strategy based on this quantitative trading research paper using Codex.
Usually, turning a research paper into something tradable means hours of reading, decoding equations, and manually implementing the strategy.
Instead, I drop the raw PDF directly into Codex.
I'm asking Codex to act like a quant researcher instead of just summarizing the paper.
Codex actually reads the methodology section, then translates it into implementable code.
Normally, this would mean stitching together signal processing libraries, reinforcement learning frameworks, and backtesting the code.
But Codex built the entire workflow automatically.
Then it ran the backtest, generated the charts, and even flagged weaknesses.
Reading quant papers is extremely useful, but having AI turn them into executable strategies in minutes?
That's where things get interesting.
